claim: Synovium is home to immune and stromal cell types that orchestrate inflammation following a joint injury.
source: Synovium is home to immune and stromal cell types that orchestrate inflammation following a joint injury; in particular, macrophages are central protagonists in this process.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the study context.

claim: Macrophages are central protagonists in orchestrating inflammation following joint injury.
source: Synovium is home to immune and stromal cell types that orchestrate inflammation following a joint injury; in particular, macrophages are central protagonists in this process.
evidence: This statement is supported by the study's focus and findings regarding macrophage roles.

claim: Immune cell types are broadly represented in healthy synovium.
source: Immune cell types are broadly represented in healthy synovium, but experience drastic expansion and speciation in PTOA, most notably in the macrophage portion.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq and flow cytometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Immune cells experience drastic expansion and speciation in PTOA.
source: Immune cell types are broadly represented in healthy synovium, but experience drastic expansion and speciation in PTOA, most notably in the macrophage portion.
evidence: This is supported by the scRNA-seq data showing increased cell numbers and diversity after injury.

claim: Macrophages experience the most notable expansion and speciation in PTOA among immune cell types.
source: Immune cell types are broadly represented in healthy synovium, but experience drastic expansion and speciation in PTOA, most notably in the macrophage portion.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data showing macrophage abundance in Figure 1C.

claim: Several polarization states of macrophages exist in synovium following joint injury.
source: We identified several polarization states of macrophages in synovium following joint injury, underpinned by distinct transcriptomic signatures, and regulated in part by stromal-derived macrophage colony-stimulating factor signaling.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq clustering and trajectory analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Macrophage polarization states are underpinned by distinct transcriptomic signatures.
source: We identified several polarization states of macrophages in synovium following joint injury, underpinned by distinct transcriptomic signatures, and regulated in part by stromal-derived macrophage colony-stimulating factor signaling.
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Macrophage polarization states are regulated in part by stromal-derived macrophage colony-stimulating factor signaling.
source: We identified several polarization states of macrophages in synovium following joint injury, underpinned by distinct transcriptomic signatures, and regulated in part by stromal-derived macrophage colony-stimulating factor signaling.
evidence: This is supported by CellChat analysis and expression data in Figure 5.

claim: The transcription factors Pu.1, Cebpα, Cebpβ, and Jun are predicted to control differentiation of systemically derived monocytes into pro-inflammatory synovial macrophages.
source: The transcription factors Pu.1, Cebpα, Cebpβ, and Jun were predicted to control differentiation of systemically derived monocytes into pro-inflammatory synovial macrophages.
evidence: This is based on RcisTarget computational analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Early studies of diet-induced obesity in mice showed recruitment of pro-inflammatory macrophages to adipose tissue from circulating monocytes.
source: For instance, early studies of diet-induced obesity in mice showed recruitment of pro-inflammatory macrophages to adipose tissue from circulating monocytes (Lumeng et al., 2007b; Lumeng et al., 2007a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: In systemic sclerosis, interactions between distinct macrophage subsets and fibroblasts drive them to adopt pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic phenotypes that underpin disease progression.
source: In systemic sclerosis, interactions between distinct macrophage subsets and fibroblasts drive them to adopt pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic phenotypes, respectively, that underpin disease progression (Fang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Osteopontin produced by pathologic SPP1+ macrophages promotes production of type I collagen by skin fibroblasts.
source: Specifically, osteopontin produced by pathologic SPP1+ macrophages promotes production of type I collagen by skin fibroblasts (Gao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Fibroblasts in sclerotic lesions produce high levels of TLR4 that drive persistent fibrosis.
source: Fibroblasts in sclerotic lesions produce high levels of TLR4 that drive persistent fibrosis (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The synovium is a heterogenous connective tissue in joints, populated with immune cells, vascular and lymphatic endothelial cells, fibroblasts, adipocytes, and other mesenchymal-lineage stromal cells.
source: The synovium is a heterogenous connective tissue in joints, populated with immune cells, vascular and lymphatic endothelial cells, fibroblasts, adipocytes, and other mesenchymal-lineage stromal cells (Lieberthal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a general anatomical description supported by citation.

claim: Synovium is increasingly recognized as a principal regulator of intra-articular inflammation in osteoarthritis.
source: Synovium is increasingly recognized as a principal regulator of intra-articular inflammation in osteoarthritis (OA), given its highly vascularized nature and abundance of resident immune cells compared to tissues such as meniscus and cartilage.
evidence: This claim reflects current understanding in the field.

claim: Synovial inflammation is a pathologic driver of OA.
source: Synovial inflammation, now appreciated as a pathologic driver of OA (Atukorala et al., 2016; Sanchez-Lopez et al., 2022; Knights et al., 2023b), is characterized by expansion of resident synovial fibroblasts and immune cells as well as influx of systemically derived immune cells; however, we have a limited understanding of the cellular, molecular, and temporal mechanisms of these interactions, and how they differ or correspond across forms of arthritis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Synovial inflammation is characterized by expansion of resident synovial fibroblasts and immune cells as well as influx of systemically derived immune cells.
source: Synovial inflammation, now appreciated as a pathologic driver of OA (Atukorala et al., 2016; Sanchez-Lopez et al., 2022; Knights et al., 2023b), is characterized by expansion of resident synovial fibroblasts and immune cells as well as influx of systemically derived immune cells; however, we have a limited understanding of the cellular, molecular, and temporal mechanisms of these interactions, and how they differ or correspond across forms of arthritis.
evidence: This is a general characterization of synovial inflammation.

claim: The specific roles of distinct activated immune cell populations in orchestrating synovial inflammation have been well characterized in the context of rheumatoid arthritis.
source: The specific roles of distinct activated immune cell populations in orchestrating synovial inflammation have been well characterized in the context of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (Weyand and Goronzy, 2021; Alivernini et al., 2020), providing valuable insights of disease pathogenesis and advancing therapeutic efficacies (Udalova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on RA.

claim: Macrophage ablation in mice by clodronate liposomes yielded generally favorable OA outcomes, including reduced osteophyte formation.
source: Macrophage ablation in mice by clodronate liposomes yielded generally favorable OA outcomes, including reduced osteophyte formation (Blom et al., 2007; Blom et al., 2004), however pharmacogenetic macrophage depletion using the MaFIA mouse resulted in systemic inflammation, exacerbated immune influx into the joint, with no attenuation of OA severity (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Pharmacogenetic macrophage depletion using the MaFIA mouse resulted in systemic inflammation, exacerbated immune influx into the joint, with no attenuation of OA severity.
source: Macrophage ablation in mice by clodronate liposomes yielded generally favorable OA outcomes, including reduced osteophyte formation (Blom et al., 2007; Blom et al., 2004), however pharmacogenetic macrophage depletion using the MaFIA mouse resulted in systemic inflammation, exacerbated immune influx into the joint, with no attenuation of OA severity (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Synovial macrophages play critical physiological functions such as the timely clearance of apoptotic cells.
source: Indeed, synovial macrophages play critical physiological functions such as the timely clearance of apoptotic cells, which is impaired in OA (Del Sordo et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Clearance of apoptotic cells by synovial macrophages is impaired in OA.
source: Indeed, synovial macrophages play critical physiological functions such as the timely clearance of apoptotic cells, which is impaired in OA (Del Sordo et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: In a model of inflammatory arthritis, resolution requires the suppression of pro-inflammatory, systemically derived F4/80hi MHC Class II+ macrophages.
source: In a model of inflammatory arthritis, Huang et al. showed that resolution requires the suppression of pro-inflammatory, systemically derived F4/80hi MHC Class II+ macrophages and that macrophages with a resident-like phenotype promote inflammatory resolution (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Macrophages with a resident-like phenotype promote inflammatory resolution in inflammatory arthritis.
source: In a model of inflammatory arthritis, Huang et al. showed that resolution requires the suppression of pro-inflammatory, systemically derived F4/80hi MHC Class II+ macrophages and that macrophages with a resident-like phenotype promote inflammatory resolution (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The ACLR model recapitulates traumatic joint injury.
source: In this study, we employed a non-invasive anterior cruciate ligament rupture (ACLR) model of PTOA that recapitulates traumatic joint injury (Christiansen et al., 2012; Maerz et al., 2015) to dissect the dynamic immune cell environment in PTOA synovium, with a focus on the early post-injury period.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work describing the model.

claim: The ACLR model avoids the need for surgery and its confounding effects on synovial inflammation.
source: Importantly, the ACLR model avoids the need for surgery and its confounding effects on synovial inflammation.
evidence: This is a stated advantage of the model used in the study.

claim: Abundance of synovial immune cells greatly increased acutely after injury (7 days ACLR).
source: Abundance of synovial immune cells greatly increased acutely after injury (7 days ACLR), with a degree of resolution occurring by 28 days ACLR (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: A degree of resolution of immune cell abundance occurs by 28 days ACLR.
source: Abundance of synovial immune cells greatly increased acutely after injury (7 days ACLR), with a degree of resolution occurring by 28 days ACLR (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Macrophages predominated both numerically and proportionally in healthy and injured synovium.
source: Macrophages, unsurprisingly, predominated both numerically and proportionally in healthy and injured synovium, with various subsets of T cells and DCs comprising most of the remaining cells (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: Various subsets of T cells and DCs comprise most of the remaining immune cells in synovium after macrophages.
source: Macrophages, unsurprisingly, predominated both numerically and proportionally in healthy and injured synovium, with various subsets of T cells and DCs comprising most of the remaining cells (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in figures.

claim: All major groups of immune cells identified in scRNA-seq were also identified by flow cytometry within the CD45+ pool of synovial cells.
source: To assess whether the immune cell types observed in scRNA-seq based on their transcriptomic signatures were detectable at the functional protein level using surface markers, we employed multi-color flow cytometry. Indeed, all major groups of immune cells were identified within the CD45+ pool of synovial cells, based on their surface marker and light scatter profiles (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Monocytes, macrophages, DCs, neutrophils, B cells, T and NK cells, mast cells, and proliferating immune cells were all detected in the integrated immune cell dataset.
source: Monocytes, macrophages, DCs, neutrophils, B cells, T and NK cells, mast cells, and proliferating immune cells were all detected, and the same, or very similar, cell types clustered closely together across datasets following integration (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrated scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The same or very similar immune cell types clustered closely together across datasets following integration.
source: Monocytes, macrophages, DCs, neutrophils, B cells, T and NK cells, mast cells, and proliferating immune cells were all detected, and the same, or very similar, cell types clustered closely together across datasets following integration (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrated UMAP plots in Figure 2.

claim: Neutrophils are known to play a larger role in RA than in PTOA.
source: This was most strikingly evident with the neutrophil clusters (Neut-1, -2, and -3) present primarily in the Sebastian and Muench datasets, the latter of which modeled RA in which neutrophils are known to play a larger role (Khandpur et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on RA.

claim: Approximately half of all CD45+ cells in digested whole knee joints are neutrophils.
source: We detected a high abundance of neutrophils in digested whole knee joints by flow cytometry – approximately half of all CD45+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Neutrophil abundance in whole joint digests was not reduced when mice were systemically perfused to clear the vasculature.
source: This number was not reduced when mice were systemically perfused to clear the vasculature, suggesting that neutrophils in the joint digest are not derived from local blood vessels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental comparison of perfused vs unperfused samples.

claim: Neutrophils in the joint digest are not derived from local blood vessels.
source: This number was not reduced when mice were systemically perfused to clear the vasculature, suggesting that neutrophils in the joint digest are not derived from local blood vessels.
evidence: This is inferred from the perfusion experiment results.

claim: Neutrophil clusters 1, 2, and 3, particularly Neut-1, are more likely bone marrow-derived than true intra-articular tissue neutrophils.
source: Comparison of the gene signatures of neutrophil clusters 1, 2, and 3 to publicly available neutrophil datasets support that these cells, particularly Neut-1, are more likely bone marrow-derived than true intra-articular tissue neutrophils (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B and C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by CIPR analysis comparing gene signatures.

claim: Myeloid cells (monocytes, macrophages, granulocytes, DCs) were the predominant cell group across datasets.
source: Across datasets, myeloid cells (monocytes, macrophages, granulocytes, DCs) were the predominant cell group, with lymphocytes (T and B cells) comprising less than 20% of total immune cells, and mast cells were very rare (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2C.

claim: Lymphocytes (T and B cells) comprise less than 20% of total immune cells across datasets.
source: Across datasets, myeloid cells (monocytes, macrophages, granulocytes, DCs) were the predominant cell group, with lymphocytes (T and B cells) comprising less than 20% of total immune cells, and mast cells were very rare (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in figures.

claim: Mast cells were very rare across datasets.
source: Across datasets, myeloid cells (monocytes, macrophages, granulocytes, DCs) were the predominant cell group, with lymphocytes (T and B cells) comprising less than 20% of total immune cells, and mast cells were very rare (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in figures.

claim: DCs and T/NK cells participate strongly in signaling via integrins, selectins, and chemokine ligands.
source: River plots of outgoing communication signals from immune cell clusters showed distinct broad signaling patterns for most immune cell types across datasets, with the notable exception of DCs and T/NK cells which were all predicted to participate strongly in signaling via integrins, selectins, and chemokine ligands (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mast cells were enriched for sending out CSF and interleukin-4 (IL-4) signals.
source: Mast cells were enriched for sending out CSF and interleukin-4 (IL-4) signals, while monocytes and macrophages were enriched for IL-1 and IGF signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by CellChat analysis of outgoing signaling patterns.

claim: Monocytes and macrophages were enriched for IL-1 and IGF signaling.
source: Mast cells were enriched for sending out CSF and interleukin-4 (IL-4) signals, while monocytes and macrophages were enriched for IL-1 and IGF signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by CellChat analysis of outgoing signaling patterns.

claim: Macrophages represented a higher proportion of cells in the inflammatory/RA datasets (Culemann and Muench) compared to PTOA datasets.
source: Macrophages represented a higher proportion of cells in the inflammatory/RA datasets (Culemann and Muench), while monocytes were more proportionally abundant in the PTOA datasets (Sebastian and Knights) (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Monocytes were more proportionally abundant in the PTOA datasets (Sebastian and Knights) compared to RA datasets.
source: Macrophages represented a higher proportion of cells in the inflammatory/RA datasets (Culemann and Muench), while monocytes were more proportionally abundant in the PTOA datasets (Sebastian and Knights) (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Osteoclasts represented <5% of cells in the monocyte/macrophage subset.
source: Osteoclasts represented <5% of cells, and macrophages were vastly more abundant than monocytes or osteoclast-like cells in both PTOA and RA models.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from the integrated analysis.

claim: Macrophages were vastly more abundant than monocytes or osteoclast-like cells in both PTOA and RA models.
source: Osteoclasts represented <5% of cells, and macrophages were vastly more abundant than monocytes or osteoclast-like cells in both PTOA and RA models.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from the integrated analysis.

claim: 85 differentially expressed genes were found exclusively between PTOA and control macrophages.
source: 85 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were found exclusively between PTOA and control macrophages, 89 DEGs were found exclusively in the RA vs control comparison, and 21 DEGs overlapped between both analyses (Figure 3E, Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 89 differentially expressed genes were found exclusively in the RA vs control macrophage comparison.
source: 85 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were found exclusively between PTOA and control macrophages, 89 DEGs were found exclusively in the RA vs control comparison, and 21 DEGs overlapped between both analyses (Figure 3E, Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 21 differentially expressed genes overlapped between PTOA vs control and RA vs control macrophage comparisons.
source: 85 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were found exclusively between PTOA and control macrophages, 89 DEGs were found exclusively in the RA vs control comparison, and 21 DEGs overlapped between both analyses (Figure 3E, Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In PTOA macrophages, collagen metabolism, myeloid differentiation regulation, neutrophil chemotaxis, and glial cell apoptosis pathways were all enriched compared to controls.
source: In PTOA macrophages, compared to controls, collagen metabolism, myeloid differentiation regulation, neutrophil chemotaxis, and glial cell apoptosis pathways were all enriched (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In RA macrophages, response to corticotropin-releasing hormone, Th1 differentiation, and cellular response to mercury were all perturbed compared to controls.
source: In RA macrophages on the other hand, response to corticotropin-releasing hormone (known to be pro-inflammatory and enriched in RA synovial fluid; Malysheva et al., 2012), Th1 differentiation, and cellular response to mercury were all perturbed (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Corticotropin-releasing hormone is known to be pro-inflammatory and enriched in RA synovial fluid.
source: In RA macrophages on the other hand, response to corticotropin-releasing hormone (known to be pro-inflammatory and enriched in RA synovial fluid; Malysheva et al., 2012), Th1 differentiation, and cellular response to mercury were all perturbed (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cytokine activity, white blood cell chemotaxis and migration, and signaling receptor activity pathways are enriched in both RA and PTOA macrophages.
source: Analysis of enriched pathways common between RA and PTOA macrophages yielded unsurprising results, including cytokine activity, white blood cell chemotaxis and migration, and signaling receptor activity (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis of common DEGs shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Sham synovium was predominated by macrophages expressing Timd4, Lyve1, and Folr2, termed basal resident macrophages.
source: Sham synovium was predominated by macrophages expressing Timd4, Lyve1, and Folr2 which we have termed basal resident macrophages, given their resemblance to homeostatic macrophages residing in various tissues with the same gene expression signature (Chakarov et al., 2019; Dick et al., 2022; Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and comparison to published signatures.

claim: Basal resident macrophages resemble homeostatic macrophages residing in various tissues with the same gene expression signature.
source: Sham synovium was predominated by macrophages expressing Timd4, Lyve1, and Folr2 which we have termed basal resident macrophages, given their resemblance to homeostatic macrophages residing in various tissues with the same gene expression signature (Chakarov et al., 2019; Dick et al., 2022; Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work describing similar macrophage populations.

claim: After injury, there was a profound increase in cellular abundance and heterogeneity of macrophages.
source: After injury, there was a profound increase in cellular abundance and heterogeneity, but with the notable loss of cells characterized by the basal resident gene signature.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing changes after ACLR.

claim: After injury, there was a notable loss of cells characterized by the basal resident gene signature.
source: After injury, there was a profound increase in cellular abundance and heterogeneity, but with the notable loss of cells characterized by the basal resident gene signature.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Trajectory modeling indicates that basal resident macrophages polarized into distinct phenotypes in PTOA, characterized by expression of Mrc1, Ly6e, and Gas6 (resident-like A) or Cd9, Spp1, and Trem2 (resident-like B).
source: Trajectory modeling using Monocle3 indicated that basal resident macrophages polarized into distinct phenotypes in PTOA, characterized by expression of Mrc1, Ly6e, and Gas6 (resident-like A) or Cd9, Spp1, and Trem2 (resident-like B) (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is based on computational trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Resident-like A macrophages were enriched for functions pertaining to complement activation and cell migration compared to basal resident macrophages.
source: Compared to basal resident macrophages, the resident-like A cluster was enriched for functions pertaining to complement activation and cell migration (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Resident-like B macrophages had enriched CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling and production of macrophage inflammatory protein, compared to basal resident cells.
source: Resident-like B cells had enriched CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling and production of macrophage inflammatory protein, compared to the basal resident cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis of DEGs.

claim: Basal resident macrophages had functional enrichment of homeostatic biological pathways including phagocytosis, endocytosis, and apoptosis compared to polarized resident-like subsets.
source: On the other hand, compared to the two polarized resident-like macrophage subsets, basal resident cells had functional enrichment of homeostatic biological pathways including phagocytosis, endocytosis, and apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The resident-like A subset was enriched for antigen presentation functions compared to resident-like B.
source: The resident-like A subset was enriched for antigen presentation functions compared to resident-like B.
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis of DEGs.

claim: Monocytes expressing Ly6c2, Plac8, and Chil3 were present, particularly after injury.
source: Monocytes expressing Ly6c2, Plac8, and Chil3 were also present, particularly after injury, and trajectory analysis suggested that they give rise to a pro-inflammatory cluster expressing Ccr2 and genes encoding MHC Class II, which we have termed infiltrating macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and trajectory analysis.

claim: Trajectory analysis suggests that monocytes give rise to a pro-inflammatory cluster expressing Ccr2 and genes encoding MHC Class II, termed infiltrating macrophages.
source: Monocytes expressing Ly6c2, Plac8, and Chil3 were also present, particularly after injury, and trajectory analysis suggested that they give rise to a pro-inflammatory cluster expressing Ccr2 and genes encoding MHC Class II, which we have termed infiltrating macrophages.
evidence: This claim is based on computational trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Genes historically used to mark 'M1' or 'M2' macrophages did not segregate neatly into defined clusters.
source: Genes historically used to mark 'M1' or 'M2' macrophages, including Tnf (encoding TNF-α) and Il10 (encoding IL-10), did not segregate neatly into defined clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D), emphasizing the need to supersede these outdated terms with more nuanced characterizations based on their in vivo gene expression and functional profiles.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The M-CSF pathway was highly induced after injury, but primarily in the stromal-to-immune direction.
source: The M-CSF pathway, involving the ligands M-CSF (macrophage colony-stimulating factor) and IL-34, and the M-CSF receptor, was highly induced after injury, but primarily in the stromal-to-immune direction (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-F), implying that stromal-derived ligands regulate synovial immune cells expressing the M-CSF receptor – namely, macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Stromal-derived ligands regulate synovial immune cells expressing the M-CSF receptor, namely macrophages.
source: The M-CSF pathway, involving the ligands M-CSF (macrophage colony-stimulating factor) and IL-34, and the M-CSF receptor, was highly induced after injury, but primarily in the stromal-to-immune direction (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-F), implying that stromal-derived ligands regulate synovial immune cells expressing the M-CSF receptor – namely, macrophages.
evidence: This is inferred from the directionality of M-CSF signaling and receptor expression patterns.

claim: M-CSF and its receptor are well recognized for their role in monocyte and macrophage function.
source: M-CSF and its receptor are well recognized for their role in monocyte and macrophage function (Lin et al., 2019; Guilliams et al., 2020), and more recently, IL-34 was identified as an alternative M-CSF ligand (Ma et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: IL-34 was identified as an alternative M-CSF ligand.
source: M-CSF and its receptor are well recognized for their role in monocyte and macrophage function (Lin et al., 2019; Guilliams et al., 2020), and more recently, IL-34 was identified as an alternative M-CSF ligand (Ma et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bulk RNA-seq of synovium showed robust induction of Csf1, Il34, and Csf1r after joint injury.
source: Bulk RNA-seq of synovium showed robust induction of Csf1 (encoding M-CSF), Il34 (encoding IL-34), and Csf1r (encoding the M-CSF receptor) after joint injury (Figure 5C); thus, we sought to determine the cell types orchestrating this signaling axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In Sham synovium, lining and sublining fibroblasts, as well as pericytes, were the primary producers of M-CSF and/or IL-34 ligand.
source: In Sham synovium, lining and sublining fibroblasts, as well as pericytes, were the primary producers of M-CSF and/or IL-34 ligand, with macrophages and DCs being the primary signal-receiving cell types (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by CellChat hierarchy plots shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In Sham synovium, macrophages and DCs were the primary signal-receiving cell types for M-CSF pathway signaling.
source: In Sham synovium, lining and sublining fibroblasts, as well as pericytes, were the primary producers of M-CSF and/or IL-34 ligand, with macrophages and DCs being the primary signal-receiving cell types (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by CellChat hierarchy plots shown in Figure 5D.

claim: After injury, there were more M-CSF pathway interactions with higher probabilities, which originated from fibroblasts and pericytes and signaled toward myeloid cells.
source: After injury, alongside the increased cell type diversity, there were more M-CSF pathway interactions (number of connections) with higher probabilities (thickness of connections), which, again, originated from fibroblasts and pericytes and signaled toward myeloid cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by CellChat hierarchy plots in Figure 5D.

claim: A small population of mast cells sent outgoing M-CSF signals at 7 days ACLR only.
source: A small population of mast cells also sent outgoing signals at 7 days ACLR only.
evidence: This claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No immune-to-stromal signaling via the M-CSF pathway was predicted.
source: No immune-to-stromal signaling via the M-CSF pathway was predicted (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fibroblasts are the major source of Csf1 ligand in synovium.
source: Expression patterns of M-CSF pathway genes in synovial cell types confirmed fibroblasts as the major source of Csf1 ligand, with no expression seen in immune cells (except for mast cells); pericytes were the primary source of Il34 ligand; and Csf1r expression was confined to the immune cell compartment (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Pericytes were the primary source of Il34 ligand in synovium.
source: Expression patterns of M-CSF pathway genes in synovial cell types confirmed fibroblasts as the major source of Csf1 ligand, with no expression seen in immune cells (except for mast cells); pericytes were the primary source of Il34 ligand; and Csf1r expression was confined to the immune cell compartment (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Csf1r expression was confined to the immune cell compartment in synovium.
source: Expression patterns of M-CSF pathway genes in synovial cell types confirmed fibroblasts as the major source of Csf1 ligand, with no expression seen in immune cells (except for mast cells); pericytes were the primary source of Il34 ligand; and Csf1r expression was confined to the immune cell compartment (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Pu.1 controls expression of Csf1r.
source: The gene regulatory network for these TFs (Figure 6E) showed distinct (e.g. Il10, Rel, Tlr7, Egr2) and shared (e.g. Vegfa, Irf2, Il6ra, Nlrp3) target genes, with Pu.1 controlling expression of Csf1r as has been described in other settings (Zhang et al., 1994; Aikawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene regulatory network analysis and citations to prior work.

claim: Expression of genes encoding Pu.1, Cebpα, Cebpβ, and Jun was not necessarily induced over pseudotime.
source: Expression of the genes encoding Pu.1, Cebpα, Cebpβ, and Jun was not necessarily induced over pseudotime, however their gene targets (derived from modules 1, 4, and 6), such as Il10, Csf1r, and Tlr7, showed increasing expression with pseudotime (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime regression plots shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Gene targets of Pu.1, Cebpα, Cebpβ, and Jun, such as Il10, Csf1r, and Tlr7, showed increasing expression with pseudotime.
source: Expression of the genes encoding Pu.1, Cebpα, Cebpβ, and Jun was not necessarily induced over pseudotime, however their gene targets (derived from modules 1, 4, and 6), such as Il10, Csf1r, and Tlr7, showed increasing expression with pseudotime (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime regression plots shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Chronic synovitis drives various pathological processes associated with arthritis, including pain and tissue damage.
source: Chronic synovitis is recognized to drive various pathological processes associated with arthritis, including pain and tissue damage, but the early cellular and molecular events following joint injury are not well described.
evidence: This is a general statement about the role of synovitis in arthritis.

claim: Synovial fibroblasts expand rapidly and phenotypically diverge into distinct functional subsets in PTOA.
source: We recently demonstrated that synovial fibroblasts expand rapidly and phenotypically diverge into distinct functional subsets in PTOA, alongside pathological activation of canonical Wnt signaling (Knights et al., 2023a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling is pathologically activated in PTOA synovium.
source: We recently demonstrated that synovial fibroblasts expand rapidly and phenotypically diverge into distinct functional subsets in PTOA, alongside pathological activation of canonical Wnt signaling (Knights et al., 2023a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Most immune cells are rare in healthy synovium.
source: The present work demonstrates the injury-induced immune cell dynamics concurrent with the activation of synovial fibroblasts, and our flow cytometric and transcriptomic analyses demonstrate that while most immune cells are rare in healthy synovium, joint injury causes massive diversification and influx of immune subsets.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's flow cytometry and scRNA-seq data.

claim: Joint injury causes massive diversification and influx of immune subsets.
source: The present work demonstrates the injury-induced immune cell dynamics concurrent with the activation of synovial fibroblasts, and our flow cytometric and transcriptomic analyses demonstrate that while most immune cells are rare in healthy synovium, joint injury causes massive diversification and influx of immune subsets.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's flow cytometry and scRNA-seq data.

claim: A resident macrophage population polarizes into two phenotypes following injury.
source: Macrophages exhibited the greatest expansion, and our single-cell transcriptomic analyses identified a resident macrophage population that polarizes into two phenotypes following injury, in addition to an infiltrating macrophage population derived from monocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: An infiltrating macrophage population is derived from monocytes in PTOA synovium.
source: Macrophages exhibited the greatest expansion, and our single-cell transcriptomic analyses identified a resident macrophage population that polarizes into two phenotypes following injury, in addition to an infiltrating macrophage population derived from monocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Synovial stromal cells were highly active in mediating immune cell infiltration and expansion.
source: Synovial stromal cells were highly active in mediating immune cell infiltration and expansion, with unbiased modeling of stromal-immune crosstalk identifying that M-CSF signaling is among the most perturbed ligand-receptor axes after injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: M-CSF signaling is among the most perturbed ligand-receptor axes after injury.
source: Synovial stromal cells were highly active in mediating immune cell infiltration and expansion, with unbiased modeling of stromal-immune crosstalk identifying that M-CSF signaling is among the most perturbed ligand-receptor axes after injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Healthy synovia contained all major immune cell types, including rare subsets such as mast cells and T cells.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Sebastian et al., 2022; Haubruck et al., 2020; Furman et al., 2021), our transcriptomic profiling demonstrated that healthy synovia contained all major immune cell types, including rare subsets such as mast cells and T cells, and this was corroborated by flow cytometry.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq and flow cytometry data, and citations to prior work.

claim: A TLF+ (Timd4+ Lyve1+ Folr2+) resident synovial macrophage population exists in healthy tissue.
source: In healthy tissue, we identified a resident synovial macrophage population with a Timd4+ Lyve1+ Folr2+ (TLF) signature that resembled homeostatic tissue-resident macrophages described in other tissue contexts (Chakarov et al., 2019; Dick et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and comparison to published signatures.

claim: Several recent studies have corroborated the existence of a pro-fibrotic macrophage population expressing Spp1, Cd9, and Trem2 that emerges in different disease contexts.
source: Several recent studies have corroborated the existence of a pro-fibrotic macrophage population that emerges in different disease contexts (Gao et al., 2020; Alivernini et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Hoeft et al., 2023; Hill et al., 2018; Jaitin et al., 2019; Fujii et al., 2022; Ramachandran et al., 2019), expressing Spp1 (encoding osteopontin), Cd9, and Trem2, strongly suggesting that the resident-like B macrophage population we identified in PTOA synovium is functionally analogous, which is significant in light of the strong fibrotic phenotype of PTOA synovium.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The resident-like B macrophage population identified in PTOA synovium is functionally analogous to pro-fibrotic macrophages described in other disease contexts.
source: Several recent studies have corroborated the existence of a pro-fibrotic macrophage population that emerges in different disease contexts (Gao et al., 2020; Alivernini et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Hoeft et al., 2023; Hill et al., 2018; Jaitin et al., 2019; Fujii et al., 2022; Ramachandran et al., 2019), expressing Spp1 (encoding osteopontin), Cd9, and Trem2, strongly suggesting that the resident-like B macrophage population we identified in PTOA synovium is functionally analogous, which is significant in light of the strong fibrotic phenotype of PTOA synovium.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of gene signatures to published pro-fibrotic macrophages.

claim: PTOA synovium has a strong fibrotic phenotype.
source: Several recent studies have corroborated the existence of a pro-fibrotic macrophage population that emerges in different disease contexts (Gao et al., 2020; Alivernini et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Hoeft et al., 2023; Hill et al., 2018; Jaitin et al., 2019; Fujii et al., 2022; Ramachandran et al., 2019), expressing Spp1 (encoding osteopontin), Cd9, and Trem2, strongly suggesting that the resident-like B macrophage population we identified in PTOA synovium is functionally analogous, which is significant in light of the strong fibrotic phenotype of PTOA synovium.
evidence: This is stated as context for the significance of the findings.

claim: Trajectory modeling pointed toward pro-fibrotic macrophages arising from synovium-resident TLF+ macrophages after injury.
source: Our trajectory modeling pointed toward these pro-fibrotic macrophages arising from synovium-resident TLF+ macrophages after injury.
evidence: This claim is based on computational trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In liver cirrhosis, trajectory analysis suggested a monocytic origin for Spp1+ macrophages.
source: In liver cirrhosis, however, trajectory analysis suggested a monocytic origin for Spp1+ macrophages.
evidence: This is a comparison to findings in a different disease context.

claim: CD206 (Mrc1) has been shown to mediate collagen turnover.
source: The resident-like A cluster that emerged after injury expressed Mrc1 (CD206), historically associated with an anti-inflammatory and reparative phenotype, and which has been shown to mediate collagen turnover (Madsen et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Gas6 is required for efficient efferocytosis of apoptotic cells by synovial macrophages.
source: In addition, their potentially beneficial role in regulating extracellular matrix, the resident-like A population also expressed Gas6, which is required for efficient efferocytosis of apoptotic cells by synovial macrophages (Yao et al., 2023) – an important aspect of inflammatory resolution that goes awry in OA (Del Sordo et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Efferocytosis is an important aspect of inflammatory resolution that goes awry in OA.
source: In addition, their potentially beneficial role in regulating extracellular matrix, the resident-like A population also expressed Gas6, which is required for efficient efferocytosis of apoptotic cells by synovial macrophages (Yao et al., 2023) – an important aspect of inflammatory resolution that goes awry in OA (Del Sordo et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Infiltrating macrophages identified in this study are pro-inflammatory and analogous to F4/80hi MHC Class II+ macrophages described by Huang et al.
source: Huang et al. recently demonstrated in murine inflammatory arthritis that synovial inflammatory resolution is achieved, in part, by suppressing the in situ differentiation of infiltrating monocytes to an F4/80hi MHC Class II+ phenotype, which would otherwise promote chronic inflammation (Huang et al., 2021). Thus, we conclude that the monocyte-derived macrophages we identified to emerge in synovium following joint injury are pro-inflammatory and analogous to those described by Huang et al., and developing an understanding of the molecular mechanisms that promote their recruitment and differentiation following joint injury is critical.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of gene signatures and citation to prior work.

claim: Jun, Cebpα, Cebpβ, and Pu.1 have been previously attributed to regulate macrophage maturation in other disease contexts such as RA.
source: These have been previously attributed to regulate macrophage maturation in other disease contexts such as RA (Tu et al., 2023; Hannemann et al., 2017), often in concert with each other (Zhao et al., 2022), however empirical studies demonstrating whether maturation of systemically derived monocytes into inflammatory synovial macrophages during OA is dependent on these TFs are needed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: M-CSF (and its alternative ligand, IL-34) has been shown to mediate monocyte-macrophage maturation via the M-CSF receptor in other disease contexts.
source: M-CSF (and its alternative ligand, IL-34) has been shown to mediate monocyte-macrophage maturation via the M-CSF receptor in other disease contexts (Lin et al., 2019; Aikawa et al., 2010; Preisser et al., 2014), and monoclonal antibody-mediated M-CSF receptor inhibition ameliorated cytokine production in human RA synovial explants and mitigated disease severity in murine collagen-induced arthritis (Garcia et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Monoclonal antibody-mediated M-CSF receptor inhibition ameliorated cytokine production in human RA synovial explants and mitigated disease severity in murine collagen-induced arthritis.
source: M-CSF (and its alternative ligand, IL-34) has been shown to mediate monocyte-macrophage maturation via the M-CSF receptor in other disease contexts (Lin et al., 2019; Aikawa et al., 2010; Preisser et al., 2014), and monoclonal antibody-mediated M-CSF receptor inhibition ameliorated cytokine production in human RA synovial explants and mitigated disease severity in murine collagen-induced arthritis (Garcia et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Pu.1 is a putative regulator of Csf1r.
source: Our TF binding analysis revealed Pu.1 as a putative regulator of Csf1r, in agreement with previous reports (Zhang et al., 1994; Aikawa et al., 2010; Krysinska et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by RcisTarget analysis and citations to prior work.
